title: Metrics
summary: How do you compare memories? This topic defines latency and cycle time, bandwidth, density, energy and leakage, retention and endurance — with worked calculations you will need when choosing and sizing memories.
objectives: Compute peak bandwidth for on-chip and external memories.
Explain why small memories are area-inefficient.
Compare the energy of on-chip and off-chip accesses.
Use retention and endurance figures in design decisions.

blocks.md:
Two different numbers describe speed:

- **Latency** (access time): how long from the request until the data is there.
- **Cycle time**: how often a new access can start.

A pipelined memory can have a latency of 2 clocks but still accept a new access **every** clock — its cycle time is one clock.

blocks.caption: Access time across the hierarchy — note the logarithmic scale

blocks.title: Latency hurts, bandwidth helps
blocks.md: Latency cannot be hidden by making the memory wider; it is fought with caches and prefetching. Bandwidth can be bought with width, more ports or more banks.

> bandwidth = width × accesses per second × number of ports (or channels)

Worked examples:

rows: HBM2 stack, 1024 bit, 2 Gb/s per pin
blocks.caption: Peak bandwidth examples

blocks.title: Peak and sustained
blocks.md: These are **peak** numbers. Real DRAM bandwidth is lower because of row opening, refresh and bus turnarounds — often 60–90 % of the peak.

Density is bits per mm². It depends first on the **cell** — DRAM and flash pack several times more bits per area than SRAM — and then on the **overhead** around the array: decoders, sense amplifiers, column muxes, control.

The overhead is roughly fixed per memory, so **small memories are inefficient**: a 64-word memory may spend more area on its periphery than on its cells. That is why many small memories are merged into fewer large ones — or built from flip-flops.

A memory consumes:

- **dynamic energy per access** — charging word lines, bit lines and sense amplifiers; it grows with the memory size (longer lines);
- **leakage** — every cell leaks all the time, so it grows with the number of bits.

Off-chip accesses are far more expensive than on-chip ones:

blocks.caption: Energy per operation (after M. Horowitz, ISSCC 2014)

blocks.md: To save leakage, SRAM macros offer **light sleep** (periphery off), **deep sleep / retention** (lower array voltage, data kept) and **shut-down** (everything off, data lost). In RTL the enable signal already helps: `en = 0` avoids the dynamic energy of an access.

blocks.prompt: Practice: order by energy per 64-bit access, lowest first.

blocks.title: Endurance shapes the design
blocks.md: Flash controllers spread writes over all blocks (**wear levelling**) and use strong ECC. A design that writes a log entry to the same flash page every second would wear it out in about a day at 10⁵ cycles.
